text: There is no single right answer to which automation tool you should just learn and use for everything. Experienced administrators carry PowerShell, Python, and plain CLI scripting side by side, because each one is genuinely the best fit for a different kind of job. Treating this like a contest with one winner leads to a forty-line Python script where three lines of Bash would have done the job.

PowerShell is the natural choice for Windows-heavy, Azure-heavy shops. The Az module gives nearly every Azure operation a native, well-documented cmdlet — New-AzResourceGroup, Get-AzVM, Set-AzStorageAccount — and it follows the same Verb-Noun pattern this course already covered, so New-AzVM reads the same way New-Item always did.

Python earns its place when a task needs to run identically on Windows, Linux, and macOS, when the logic is genuinely complex with branching and retries, or when you need a library that has nothing to do with cloud infrastructure at all. Both major clouds ship full-featured Python SDKs, so Python is the better choice specifically once a script needs to do more than call cloud APIs in a straight line.

Sometimes the job really is just running a handful of CLI commands in order, with one piece of output feeding the next. A short Bash script calling az or aws directly is often faster to write and easier for a teammate to read, because there is no module to import and no SDK syntax to look up.

It is also the most portable option of the three: a Bash script using the az or aws CLI runs the same way on a Linux build server, a Mac laptop, or WSL on Windows, with nothing extra installed beyond the CLI itself. Chapter 4 builds real examples of exactly this kind of script.
Up next: idempotency, and why a script should be safe to run twice without duplicating resources or erroring out on the second run.
